item.title: Distributed Neural Dynamics Underlie the Shift from Movement Preparation to Execution.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
Understanding how neural population activity supports the transition from movement preparation to execution remains a central challenge in systems neuroscience. Invasive recordings in nonhuman primates indicate that motor preparation and execution occupy orthogonal subspaces within the primary motor cortex (M1), yet how these neural dynamics evolve across broader networks and support skilled, memory-guided action remains poorly understood. We used source-resolved magnetoencephalography during a memory-guided finger-sequence task to track population dynamics across a cortico-hippocampal network. Manifold trajectories and decoding revealed that preparation and execution of movement sequences occupy distinct, yet not fully orthogonal, neural subspaces-a separation that generalized across all regions but was most pronounced in motor regions. Crucially, we identified a hierarchical spatio-temporal transition across the brain: The state shift originated in the hippocampus via theta-band modulations and rippled through the pre-SMA, SMA, and lateral premotor areas before culminating in M1 via broadband activity. This progression follows the functional hierarchy of descending motor pathways, with M1 shifting last, 160 msec before the first button press. Although sequence identity could be decoded from all areas during execution, only the hippocampus and M1 maintained predictive representations of upcoming sequences during preparation. These findings demonstrate that the initiation of complex motor sequences relies on a well-timed integration of hippocampal memory systems with primary motor output, rather than being a process localized to the motor cortices alone.

item.title: Trust Modulates Speech Entrainment: Enhanced Cortical Tracking for Low-trust Speakers.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
Trust is a critical component of human communication, providing a foundation for understanding, information exchange, and social coordination. Much of the research on trust in speech communication has focused on how vocal characteristics impact perceived trustworthiness. However, little is known about how trust in a speaker affects the neural processing of speech. Here, we demonstrate a two-stage experimental framework to study that question using noninvasive EEG. First, participants engage in a trust-building stage, where they play an investment game with fictional characters, each paired with a distinctive voice and trustworthiness level (i.e., frequency and magnitude of lies). Next, participants engage in a story-listening stage, in which they are presented with stories from the same characters. Data acquired from 20 young adults confirm a statistically significant correlation between the perceived and actual trustworthiness of the fictional characters. Cortical speech tracking was quantified using a temporal response function analysis on the EEG data. We found that the trustworthiness established during the trust-building stage influenced the cortical tracking of speech in the subsequent story-listening stage, with lower trustworthiness corresponding to a stronger cortical tracking of speech. Interestingly, trustworthiness selectively modulated tracking strength, with no statistically significant changes in the spatial and temporal temporal response function dynamics.

item.title: The unfolding symphony: unraveling brain dynamics via data-driven multi-scale functional connectivity in task-state fMRI.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
Task-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) can characterize both regional responses and changes in statistical dependence among distributed brain systems. This narrative review examines dynamic and multiscale connectivity within a broader framework that distinguishes task-modulated functional connectivity, trial-wise covariation, effective connectivity, and data-driven state analysis. Sliding-window correlation, hidden Markov models, and co-activation patterns are compared by their data representations, temporal assumptions, and computational procedures; graph representations can be combined with each of these strategies. We discuss supervised recurrent, transformer, and graph models alongside unsupervised state discovery, self-supervised representation learning, and emerging brain foundation models. Explainability requires evaluation of model attributions, including graph masks and perturbation-based analyses, rather than anatomical plausibility alone. The spatial framework includes whole-brain networks, subnetworks, atlas-defined regions of interest, and voxel- or layer-level measurements. Proposed links across these levels remain hypotheses: faster sampling of the blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) signal does not directly resolve millisecond neural interactions, and resting-state or animal findings do not establish the corresponding mechanism during human tasks. Shared task-evoked responses, hemodynamic variability, motion, and analytical choices can all alter apparent connectivity. Progress therefore depends on matching the estimator to the scientific question, comparing against activation and static-connectivity baselines, and validating results across participants, sessions, and acquisition settings.

item.title: Subliminal beauty engages the brain's valuation circuits.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Neuroeconomic models propose that the anterior ventral striatum (aVS) and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) are key regions for computing subjective value (SV) signals that guide choice. However, the role of conscious awareness in this process remains debated. Here we examined whether SV can be automatically computed in these regions without conscious awareness. In an fMRI experiment, human participants (24 females, 5 males) viewed faces that varied in attractiveness under three conditions: (i) suppressed from awareness via continuous flash suppression (CFS), (ii) clearly visible without suppression, or (iii) absent (background only) with CFS. Participants reported trial-wise facial identity (objective) and visibility (subjective) measures of facial awareness. In a post-fMRI session, they rated the attractiveness of each face as a measure of SV. When faces were seen, task performance (d') exceeded chance and responses were faster than in absent trials. When faces were unseen, performance was at chance but responses were slower than absent trials. Neurally, seen and unseen faces elicited greater neural signal than absent trials and showed similar neural patterns in the fusiform face area (FFA). Critically, neural signal in vmPFC correlated with SV for both seen and unseen faces, with similar neural patterns. In aVS, SV-related signal was only observed for unseen faces. Furthermore, mean face-related signal in FFA correlated with SV-related signals in aVS and vmPFC for unseen faces. These findings demonstrate that SV can be automatically computed in aVS and vmPFC without conscious awareness, suggesting a neural pathway by which subliminal information can influence value-based choice.Significance statement A central question in consciousness research and decision neuroscience is whether the brain's valuation circuitry - particularly the anterior ventral striatum (aVS) and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) - can compute subjective value automatically without conscious awareness. This question is important because prevailing accounts often assume that cognitive functions supported by the prefrontal cortex require conscious awareness of task-relevant information. Using continuous flash suppression and neuroimaging, we found that faces reported unseen nevertheless evoked value-related signals in aVS and vmPFC that scaled with subjective attractiveness ratings. These findings demonstrate that subjective value can be computed automatically from social information in the absence of conscious awareness.

item.title: During natural vision, semantic novelty modulates fixation-related processing in primate cortex.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
We sample visual scenes with short gaze fixations separated by saccades. While low-level integration is known, semantic integration of foveal vision across fixations remains unclear. We hypothesized that the brain responds to changes in semantic information from one fixation to the next, and therefore postulated a neural signal associated with semantic novelty for each saccade. Novelty was measured from different layers of a deep network on foveal vision. Only semantic, and not low- or mid-level, novelty modulated frontal and occipital fixation-related potentials in male and female human scalp EEG during natural viewing of full-length movies (3.4x106 saccades). Intracranial recordings in male and female humans (9.0x104 saccades) and female non-human primates (Macaca mulatta; 3.3x104 saccades) revealed broadband high-frequency activity modulations in scene-specific ventral visual and frontal brain areas only for semantic novelty. This modulation was stronger for movies than static images, and frontal modulation occurred early alongside occipital modulation, suggesting top-down effects. This modulation of fixation-related activity with novelty suggests that foveal representations are compared between consecutive fixations to construct scene representations during natural viewing in primates.Significance statement Primate vision relies on eye movements to sample the world, yet how the brain integrates high-level meaning across these "snapshots" remains a mystery. By combining deep-learning models with massive electrophysiological datasets from humans and macaques, we show that the brain responds to changes in semantic content between fixations, but not low- or mid-level changes. We identified a "semantic novelty" signal that modulates neural activity across the primate cortex. These findings suggest visual processing is not a series of independent glimpses, but a continuous process comparing consecutive foveal information at the semantic level. This work bridges biological vision and artificial intelligence, providing a new framework for understanding how the brain maintains a coherent understanding of a dynamic world.

item.title: Broadband gamma-band EEG changes during magnetophosphene-inducing 20 Hz magnetic field stimulation.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Magnetophosphenes are visual percepts induced by extremely low-frequency magnetic fields (ELF-MF; <300 Hz), yet the EEG expression of suprathreshold magnetophosphene-inducing stimulation remains poorly characterized and is not reliably captured by classical low-frequency markers. We tested whether suprathreshold 20 Hz tAMS is accompanied by broadband high-frequency EEG changes rather than focal oscillatory effects. EEG was recorded in N=13 healthy volunteers during 20 Hz sinusoidal magnetic-field exposure delivered using transcranial alternating magnetic stimulation (tAMS) in a global-head configuration. Three conditions were analyzed: no exposure (0 mT), subthreshold (5 mT), and suprathreshold (50 mT). Gamma-band EEG power (30-80 Hz) was quantified using complementary spectral approaches, including aperiodic-adjusted gamma power. Perception reports sharply dissociated the three conditions, with frequent perception at 50 mT only. Suprathreshold stimulation was associated with spatially distributed increases in gamma-band EEG power over frontal and occipito-parietal electrodes. The differences remained partly detectable in complementary analyses using two local aperiodic-adjustment methods and did not exhibit a consistent narrowband peak, a pattern consistent with broadband high-frequency changes. No focal power change over primary occipital electrodes remained significant after Bonferroni correction. These findings identify a spatially distributed broadband high-frequency scalp EEG effect associated with the suprathreshold 50 mT condition, with the main spatial pattern strongly preserved after ICA-based removal of components classified as ocular or muscular. The effect therefore characterizes the coupled suprathreshold stimulation-perception condition; its perception specificity and physiological source remain unresolved.

item.title: Principles of coarse-scale functional organization in occipitotemporal cortex.
item.description:
Communications biology
Occipitotemporal cortex (OTC) is known to support visual object processing, yet identifying general principles underlying its coarse-scale functional organization remains challenging. Previously proposed organizational dimensions, such as animacy or real-world size, may not generalize to more diverse, naturalistic stimuli and strong intercorrelations of object properties complicate determining which dimensions, if any, dominate OTC organization. We addressed these challenges through detailed analyses of the cortical topography underlying 15 object properties, using fMRI responses to thousands of natural images, focusing on animacy and size given their established prominence. Our results confirm many characteristics of the purported animacy-size organization, but reveal distinctions that challenge dominant notions of this organization, highlighting the importance of generalizing to large-scale naturalistic data. Beyond animacy and size, many properties could alternatively serve as organizational dimensions, yet none emerges as clearly dominant throughout OTC. Together, our findings reveal a more refined animacy-size organization than previously assumed and highlight challenges of assigning individual principles to account for OTC organization.

item.title: Creative cognition in frontotemporal dementia and brain health.
item.description:
Trends in neurosciences
Creative cognition is central to human thought and is affected by brain disease. Recent findings by Altmayer and colleagues link creative impairment in frontotemporal dementia to rostral prefrontal functional differentiation. These findings motivate a framework for investigating network coordination, circuit physiology, experience-dependent plasticity, and bodily and social regulation in creativity and health.

item.title: The Separation-Distress Network as a Transdiagnostic Mechanism Linking Relational Adversity, Social Pain, and Psychopathology.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Relational trauma is a major contributor to the development of mental health disorders. This association likely reflects the social nature of humans and other mammals, whose survival depends on maintaining stable social bonds. When these bonds are threatened or disrupted, individuals experience social pain, a distress response mediated by the mammalian separation-distress network. During early development, this network is sensitive to maintaining proximity with caregivers, as independent survival is not yet possible. Converging evidence from ethology, psychodynamic and attachment theory, and social and affective neuroscience supports the function of this network. Because mammalian brains are inherently tuned to form social bonds, adverse relational experiences can disrupt socioemotional development and increase vulnerability to psychopathology. Neural substrates of separation distress include the anterior cingulate cortex, ventral septum, bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, dorsal preoptic area, dorsomedial thalamus, and periaqueductal gray, with endogenous opioids and glucocorticoids serving as key neurochemical modulators in the separation-distress response. Separation distress and adverse relational experiences also alter physiological systems implicated in psychopathology, including the HPA axis, autonomic nervous system activity, inflammation, and brain structure and connectivity. This paper argues that relational trauma and social pain are mediated by an evolutionarily conserved subcortical separation-distress network shared across predominantly mammalian species. Dysregulation of this network may represent one common mechanism underlying depression, social anxiety, suicidality, substance use disorders, borderline personality disorder, and other psychiatric conditions. Understanding the processes linking adverse relational experiences, separation-distress activation, and social pain may provide insights into the etiology and treatment of diverse disorders.

item.title: Expectation-driven gain modulation of preparatory spatial attention.
item.description:
eLife
The visual system can flexibly adjust attentional deployment to match task demands, but whether observers can proactively modulate the spatial scope of attention based on expectations about upcoming search difficulty remains unclear. According to the zoom lens model, attention can narrow or broaden its spatial extent, with narrower focus enhancing processing efficiency, a mechanism that would benefit target discrimination in crowded displays. We tested whether observers adjust attentional scope when expecting sparse versus dense search arrays by combining spatial cueing with block-wise manipulations of display density expectations. Participants performed a visual search task in which endogenous cues predicted target location, while blocks predominantly contained either sparse (1 target, 3 distractors) or dense (1 target, 7 distractors) displays. We applied inverted encoding models to broadband EEG data to reconstruct spatial channel tuning functions, enabling precise characterization of both the locus and breadth of attentional deployment. Behaviorally, expecting difficult searches selectively improved accuracy at cued locations without costs elsewhere. Consistent with this selective benefit, neural measurements revealed that expectancy enhanced the amplitude of spatially selective responses at the attended location but did not alter tuning width. These findings demonstrate that expectations about search difficulty modulate attention through gain-based signal enhancement rather than adjustments to spatial scope, revealing that preparatory attentional control operates via amplitude modulation within a stable spatial focus. This mechanism complements reactive attentional adjustments and provides an efficient means for the visual system to optimize processing under predictable task demands.

item.title: Learning rapidly reshapes brain microstructure: evidence from dense temporal sampling of diffusion MRI.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Learning is associated with rapid microstructural changes in the human brain, yet the precise temporal dynamics of these changes remain unclear. Using dense temporal sampling of diffusion-weighted MRI (DW-MRI) combined with task-based fMRI, we assessed microstructural changes throughout a declarative learning paradigm and subsequent rest. Seventy-four participants (36 females) learned image-location associations across four encoding-retrieval repetitions while undergoing interleaved functional and DW-MRI acquisitions. A matched control group (N=37, 21 females) underwent a similar imaging protocol without learning. Dense sampling of DW-MRI acquisitions (2146 images across 22 time points in 127 min) revealed that learning-induced mean diffusivity (MD) decreases emerged shortly after learning onset and continued to develop during post-learning rest. The most robust change was localized to the left middle occipital/temporal gyrus, a region also showing functional activation during encoding and retrieval. Linear mixed-effects modeling further confirmed a significant group-by-time interaction, with MD reductions in the left middle occipital/temporal gyrus emerging as early as ≈7 min after learning onset, becoming robust by ≈35-40 min, and persisting throughout the extended post-learning period, while controls showed no changes. Our findings demonstrate that learning-related microstructural plasticity unfolds continuously from encoding to offline consolidation, with learning-induced structural changes emerging in functionally engaged regions. Dense temporal sampling of DW-MRI offers a powerful approach to bridge functional activation and structural remodeling, providing evidence of when and where experience-dependent plasticity occurs during memory formation.Significance Statement How quickly does the brain's structure change when we learn? Using dense temporal sampling of diffusion-weighted MRI (DW-MRI; 2146 images) across more than 2 hours, we show that microstructural plasticity arises rapidly during learning and continues to develop during post-learning rest. These learning-induced changes are spatially precise and overlap with task-related functional activity. By capturing the entire progression of microstructural plasticity across the learning process, rather than just before and after a learning paradigm, our study provides insights into when and where learning-induced plasticity occurs, demonstrating that memory formation involves rapid, ongoing microstructural changes in functionally engaged regions.

item.title: Spatially localized fMRI metrics as predictive and highly distinct state-independent fingerprints.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Precision medicine and the investigation of brain-behavior associations require biomarkers that are stable (low intraindividual variability) and unique (high-interindividual variability) at the same time, hence calling them "fingerprints". The functional connectome (FC) has good "fingerprint properties", as individuals can be accurately identified in a database based on their FC. Importantly, research has shown lower intraindividual variability of more localized measures of brain function, such as regional homogeneity (ReHo) and (fractional) amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations ((f)ALFF), compared with the FC. Additionally, the predictiveness of behavior using the FC is modest at best. Here, with fMRI data from two publicly available datasets, we demonstrate that individuals can be identified with near-perfect accuracies using local functional fingerprints, especially the regional homogeneity (ReHo) fingerprint. Further analyses reveal that the dorsal attention network contributes most to the individual "uniqueness" of the ReHo fingerprint. Moreover, using a machine learning setup, we find that intraindividual variability of the ReHo fingerprint across sessions shows predictive signal for individual-level intelligence, albeit with model performance dependent on the condition. Last, using two other publicly available datasets, clinical applicability is demonstrated with high fingerprint accuracies and a significant correlation between fingerprint stability and intelligence in individuals with schizophrenia. Altogether, our findings suggest that the ReHo fingerprint is a good candidate for further exploration of applicability in precision medicine.

item.title: Cortical depth EEG-fMRI at 7T: Experimental setup and analysis pipeline to elucidate generating mechanisms of alpha oscillations.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Alpha band (8-13 Hz) electroencephalography (EEG) oscillations are central to cognition, but their generating mechanisms are poorly understood. Most laminar studies investigating origins of alpha oscillations rely on invasive animal intracranial recordings. To relate these findings to human alpha generation, non-invasive techniques need to be developed. Ultra-high-field (UHF, 7T) laminar functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) enables cortical depth resolved brain responses, and, combined with simultaneous EEG, offers new insight into human alpha generation mechanisms. This work presents a framework for studying the generating mechanisms of electrophysiological signals non-invasively in humans using simultaneous EEG laminar fMRI. Data were acquired on 10 participants during an eyes-closed/eyes-open paradigm. In 9 of 10 participants, the quality of EEG and Blood Oxygenation Level Dependent (BOLD) fMRI data were sufficient to observe a significant negative correlation between EEG alpha power and the BOLD signal in visual cortex grey matter. To improve depth specificity and mitigate pial-surface BOLD signal increases due to draining veins, we applied "deveining". The effects of each of the deveining analysis steps on the cortical depth profiles of the negative alpha-BOLD correlations were studied. The largest effect arose from excluding voxels in the tissue immediately surrounding veins. After deveining, the negative alpha-BOLD correlations were significantly weaker in the middle cortical depths than in superficial and deep depths. This depth dependence was absent when modelling the task with a boxcar regressor rather than EEG alpha power, suggesting specificity to spontaneous electrophysiological (alpha) fluctuations. In conclusion, we have established a method to non-invasively interrogate the origins of electrophysiological signals. Our alpha-BOLD depth profiles during the eyes-open/eyes-closed task (strongest correlations in superficial and deep layers) are consistent with activity in cortical depths typically associated with feedback/top-down processing, but we cannot definitively demonstrate causality from these data.

item.title: Respiratory phase orchestrates human olfactory cortical dynamics.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Olfaction is fundamental to perception, memory, and emotion, yet the neural basis of human odor processing remains poorly understood. We demonstrate that odor-evoked brain activity is organized by respiratory phase-not absolute time-revealing that natural breathing structures olfactory cortical dynamics. Using simultaneous nasal respiration and electroencephalography recordings in [Formula: see text] participants, we delivered naturalistic odors (peppermint, oregano, and grapefruit) synchronized to individual breathing cycles. Odor presentation elicited respiratory phase-locked event-related spectral perturbations (RPL-ERSPs) in frontal and temporal regions, emerging during the first breath after stimulus onset. The most discriminative neural signatures were theta-band activity during inhalation and alpha-band activity during exhalation, patterns that were obscured in traditional time-locked analyses due to natural variability in breath duration. Leave-one-subject-out cross-validation of RPL-ERSPs achieved reliable odor detection (peppermint: AUC [Formula: see text] 0.79; oregano: AUC [Formula: see text] 0.67; grapefruit: AUC [Formula: see text] 0.62), establishing that phase-locked features generalize across individuals. To connect neural responses to perceptual experience without relying on odor naming-which can be disproportionately impaired in some populations-we quantified odor recognition using free-response descriptions scored with a semantic-similarity approach. Behavioral recognition strength paralleled the neural decoding hierarchy across odors, establishing the perceptual validity of RPL-ERSPs. RPL-ERSPs revealed rapid habituation, with decoding performance declining over repeated presentations, due to selective degradation of the most informative phase-locked features. These findings establish respiratory rhythm as a temporal scaffold for human olfactory cortical processing, positioning RPL-ERSPs as a sensitive, task-free approach for assessing olfactory function. We provide an open-source, respiration-synchronized olfactometer design to enable replication and adoption.

item.title: Constructing events across perception, action, and thought.
item.description:
Trends in neurosciences
The brain organizes continuous experience into events that structure episodic memory and guide behavior. Traditional accounts have primarily focused on sensory discontinuities and prediction errors that trigger updates of event models. Here, we broaden this view to consider event boundaries arising during goal-directed behavior, spontaneous thought, and memory recall, including transitions generated in the absence of corresponding changes in sensory input. We propose that prediction error and uncertainty provide complementary signals for event model updating: prediction errors signal a violation of current expectations, whereas uncertainty may promote updating when upcoming states become difficult to predict. We further suggest that the hippocampus may serve as a candidate hub linking boundary-related representational changes across perception, action, and thought. Together, this framework offers an integrative account of how the brain detects and generates event structure in continuous experience to support memory and behavior.

item.title: Consumer neuroscience: the emerging science of everyday choices.
item.description:
Trends in cognitive sciences
Consumer neuroscience is a developing field at the intersection of neuroscience, psychology, economics, and marketing that seeks to uncover the neural and physiological mechanisms underlying consumer behavior. Building on early psychophysiological studies, the field has expanded substantially since the mid-2000s through an increasing range of methods and models. We highlight that its strength lies in spanning multiple levels of analysis to address marketing-relevant questions. We highlight four major trends driving the field: improving behavioral prediction, synthesizing evidence through multidataset analyses, developing formal models linking neural processes to consumer decision-making, and integrating brain and body measures. Together, these advances position consumer neuroscience as an integrative science with implications for marketing, policy, and consumer welfare.

item.title: Beyond Scene Construction: Mind Time and the Temporal Organisation of Cognition across Hippocampal-Cortical Systems.
item.description:
Neuropsychologia
Scene-construction theory explains how spatially coherent event models support memory and imagination, although parts of their temporal organisation are less fully specified. Mind Time brings scene construction into relation with temporal-context and self-location research, drawing on autobiographical memory and navigation to explain how events are related to one another and to a selected temporal origin across scales. Separating these represented relations from the operations that produce and revise them accommodates evidence for a distributed hippocampal-cortical system, including temporal judgements possible despite impaired episodic construction. Comparative findings constrain inferences about component capacities without resolving claims about subjective experience. Within this integrative account, we propose that, during active construction, revising a temporal relation changes the information available to a represented self within the relevant history before a particular consequence is requested. An experiment would test whether this inferred state changes in advance and is available for use in subsequent imagination. Communication could carry the revision between people; transpersonal extended Mental Time Travel (teMTT) specifies how communication or shared records alter another person's later reconstruction or planning. Existing mental-model and predictive accounts could implement the coordination.

item.title: Working memory supports cognitive control by orchestrating dimension-specific modulation during late conflict resolution.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Working memory plays a central role in cognitive control, yet how it shapes target- and distractor-related processing over time remains unclear. Here, we combined a working memory load manipulation with a modified Stroop task in which distractors preceded targets. Behaviorally, we found that pre-exposure to the distractor eliminated the congruency effect, but this benefit was absent under high load. This pattern suggests that the benefit of advance distractor presentation is sensitive to concurrent working-memory demands. Electrophysiologically, the distractor-locked lateralized readiness potential (LRP) indicated that working-memory load altered distractor-related response activation before target onset. After target onset, load-related modulation emerged during late conflict resolution, as indexed by the sustained potential (SP), whereas earlier intervals associated with attentional selection (posterior N2) and conflict monitoring (N450) did not show load-dependent modulation. Time-frequency decoding and representational similarity analysis further revealed distinct spectro-temporal profiles of target- and distractor-related processing: target-related coding emerged earlier in the theta band (540-780 ms), consistent with stimulus-response mapping, whereas distractor-related coding emerged later in the mu-beta band (870-1180 ms), consistent with response-related regulation. These findings highlight dimension- and stage-specific patterns of working-memory modulation during conflict resolution.

item.title: Short-Video Experience and Brain-State Dynamics During the Processing of Rapidly Changing Video Information in Youth.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Background Short-video platforms frequently expose youth to rapidly changing video information. Processing such inputs requires large-scale brain networks to reorganize with the ongoing context. However, little is known about these dynamics or their association with prior short-video viewing experience. Methods A total of 108 youth aged 8-18 years completed resting-state and naturalistic movie-viewing fMRI scans. The movie comprised rapidly changing and relatively continuous segments. Hidden Markov models were applied to 17 cortical networks to identify recurrent brain states, and a joint rest-task analysis examined the context specificity of the main finding. Results Eight task-related brain states were identified. Five differed in fractional occupancy (FO) between conditions, and global switching was slightly higher during rapidly changing segments. State 7 was the only state showing an interaction with short-video viewing experience. Its FO was higher during relatively continuous than rapidly changing segments among participants reporting no prior Douyin use, whereas the condition difference was not significant among those reporting prior Douyin use. Visit frequency analyses showed a similar pattern. The interaction remained robust after covariate adjustment and was also observed in the joint rest-task analysis, with no significant group difference at rest. Conclusions Rapidly changing video information was associated with brain-state reorganization in youth. Douyin use was associated with lower State 7 occupancy during relatively continuous narrative segments; no significant group difference in the matched state's occupancy was detected at rest. These findings provide new evidence linking short-video viewing experience to context-dependent brain dynamics in youth.

item.title: Distinct neural representations of perceptual and numerical absence in the human brain.
item.description:
eLife
The ability to represent absences is fundamental to human perception and cognition. Sensitivity to non-numerical absences depends on inferring a lack of sensory evidence, enabling the recognition of a lack of environmental resources or other objects. In turn, encoding numerical absence as a concept - in the form of the number zero - has enabled a multitude of technological and mathematical advances. Whether perceptual and conceptual absences rely on overlapping or distinct neural representations in the human brain, however, remains unknown. We employed three different tasks together with magnetoencephalography to characterise neural representations of absence evoked within perceptual and numerical domains. Using multivariate decoding and Bayes factor analyses, we replicate previous findings of shared representations of numerical absence across symbolic and non-symbolic formats. In contrast, we show that these representations of numerical absence are distinct from those evoked by non-numerical absences. This result held even after controlling for stimulus-level confounds which generate surface-level similarities between perceptual absences and non-symbolic empty sets. Our results extend a boundary between perception and cognition to the domain of absence and provide insight into the different mechanisms employed by the human brain to both perceive and conceive of absences.

item.title: Endogenous suspension of phenomenal consciousness during extended cessation: Regional homogeneity analysis of multi-participant 7T fMRI of an advanced meditative endpoint.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Extended cessation (EC) is a rare advanced meditative state characterized by the voluntary absence of reportable phenomenal experience, followed by reproducible aftereffects including immense mental clarity, equanimity, and peace. EC offers an endogenous model for investigating the mechanisms of consciousness. In a small-N case study (N = 3) using ultra-high-resolution 7T functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) with dense within-subject sampling, we quantified whole-brain activity and related it to chemoarchitecture and cognitive maps. EC is marked by increased activity in unimodal sensory cortices and viscerosensory brainstem nuclei, and down-regulation in transmodal regions, subcortex and brainstem. Meta-analytic cognitive decoding linked EC to perceptual clarity and attentional processes, and away from distress-related domains. Multivariate coupling to normative neurotransmitter maps revealed that EC-related connectivity changes covaried with histaminergic H3 receptors topology. These findings constrain prevailing theories of consciousness by demonstrating that loss of experience need not entail global neural suppression, and supports accounts emphasizing selective precision modulation and hierarchical decoupling. More broadly, EC demonstrates that consciousness can cease without global suppression, suggesting a potential "reset" mechanism that fosters equanimity and the potential for flourishing.

item.title: In-group neural alignment serves as a biomarker of social identity.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
In this study, we propose a perspective on neural synchronization. Beyond reflecting shared understanding between individuals, we suggest it serves as a biological marker of social homogeneity. We examined fMRI neural responses of 42 participants (21 religious, 21 secular) watching neutral and religion-relevant video narratives. While explicit measures of emotional response, agreement, and engagement showed no significant differences in within-group variance, religious participants-representing a tighter social structure-exhibited significantly higher in-group neural synchrony across all content types and brain networks. Remarkably, synchrony values predicted religious orientation with an accuracy of up to 92%. We conclude that a community's homogeneous social structure drives pervasive neural alignment, positioning neural synchrony as a potential signature of group cohesion beyond explicit behavioral measures.

item.title: Disrupting the semantic network shifts activity to domain-general brain regions.
item.description:
Nature communications
Semantic processing relies on flexible interactions between specialized lexico-semantic regions and domain-general control networks, particularly under challenging conditions. Using transcranial magnetic stimulation interleaved with functional magnetic resonance imaging, we investigated acute network adaptation when the left posterior middle temporal gyrus-a core lexico-semantic region-was perturbed during lexico-semantic decisions in 25 healthy participants. High-intensity transcranial magnetic stimulation over the posterior middle temporal gyrus induced task-specific activity increases across semantic control and lexical retrieval areas, as well as remote domain-general regions. Critically, increased local activity at the stimulation site correlated with slower reaction times, whereas greater upregulation in domain-general frontal regions was associated with less disrupted semantic performance. These findings indicate that acute semantic disruption triggers immediate, flexible recruitment of domain-general control areas consistent with the maintenance of task performance, highlighting the brain's capacity to dynamically adapt to interference. Our findings contribute to the current understanding of putative compensatory network-level mechanisms supporting lexico-semantic cognition.

item.title: Repetition Dissociates Pointer and Content-based Representations in Visual Working Memory: Contrasting the CDA with Multivariate Shape Decoding.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Memorizing a new phone number or address is hard at first, but becomes easier with repetition, as information shifts from working memory to long-term memory. Here we investigated how repetition affects the storage and transition of different aspects of mnemonic information by comparing univariate neural markers of active object storage with multivariate decoding of memory content. Thirty participants encoded lateralized stimuli from a continuous shape space into memory. Memory items were repeated six times in a row to induce learning. In line with earlier work, EEG recordings revealed that repetition led to a reduction in contralateral delay activity (CDA), a measure of active storage that has been taken to reflect a pointer-like representation of the individual object or its original source. In contrast, shape decoding during the retention and also after an impulse perturbation remained constant across repetitions. These results suggest that learning over repetitions reflects the abolishment of active and individuated object memory representations while passive, source-independent memory representations are retained.

item.title: Temporal coupling shapes the effects of prolonged muscle-tendon vibration on sensorimotor EEG activity during motor imagery.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Motor imagery (MI) recruits sensorimotor networks overlapping those engaged during physical execution and represents a promising rehabilitation tool. While concurrent afferent stimulation enhances MI-related cortical engagement, the effects of prolonged proprioceptive conditioning prior to MI remain unexplored. This study investigated whether prolonged muscle-tendon vibration (MTV) could modulate cortical activity during subsequent MI, indexed by electroencephalographic alpha- and beta-band event-related desynchronization (ERD). Twenty healthy adults performed imagined maximal isometric knee extensions before and after 20-minute suprapatellar MTV (100 Hz) or SHAM vibration (30 Hz with foam interface) in counterbalanced sessions. Cortical engagement was assessed via EEG burst detection over central electrodes (C3, Cz, C4). Maximal force capacity, submaximal force estimation performance, and cortical responses during combined MI and MTV were also evaluated. MTV induced stronger vibratory responses than SHAM, consistent with enhanced proprioceptive afferent activation. Following MTV, voluntary force outcomes showed near-threshold changes consistent with the expected direction, namely reduced maximal force capacity and altered submaximal force calibration, suggesting modified proprioceptive feedback. MI performed after MTV conditioning exhibited reduced alpha- and beta-band ERD compared to SHAM, with greater vibratory-induced responses being associated with a less pronounced post-vibration beta ERD. Conversely, when MI was performed concurrently with MTV following conditioning, alpha-band ERD increased selectively in the MTV session, with no modulation in the beta band. These findings suggest that prolonged proprioceptive conditioning modulates MI-related cortical engagement differently depending on the sensorimotor context in which imagery is performed. Such state-dependent effects may support distinct intervention strategies aimed either at recalibrating maladaptive sensorimotor patterns or at enhancing cortical recruitment in rehabilitation contexts.

item.title: A transdiagnostic model of illness awareness and denial: Core components of the broader construct of insight into illness.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Insight into illness is a dynamic multidimensional construct that varies between individuals and medical and psychiatric disorders, and influences treatment engagement and clinical outcomes. Despite extensive study, accounts remain fragmented and disorder specific. This review focuses on subjective illness awareness and proposes a hypothesis-generating neurobiological framework in which fluctuations in awareness and denial emerge from interactions among self-representational networks, hierarchical predictive processing, and salience-threat systems that shape the balance between self-model stability and adaptation to illness-related information. Illness-related stimuli generate prediction errors (i.e., mismatches between sensory input and the self-model) that may update higher-order self-beliefs when assigned sufficient precision. Conversely, denial may occur when identity-relevant psychological threat biases precision toward self-related priors, potentially shifting network dynamics toward relatively left-lateralized self-representational states that attenuate discrepant information and preserve psychological homeostasis. This probabilistic model of illness awareness depends on the strength and credibility of illness-related evidence and flexibility of higher-order self-related beliefs. The review specifies falsifiable predictions for hemispheric engagement, threat-related precision weighting, and self-specific belief updating and identifies potential therapeutic targets.

item.title: Beyond Pathology: Perivascular Spaces as Dynamic Players in Neurodevelopment and Brain Health.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Perivascular spaces (PVS) have historically been viewed as radiological markers of aging and cerebrovascular pathology. However, this narrow perspective overlooks accumulating evidence that PVS likely undergo dynamic, prolonged maturation across the lifespan and may play an essential role in healthy brain development. This Viewpoint article challenges the prevailing paradigm by positioning PVS not as passive anatomical structures or mere disease indicators, but as active participants in postnatal neurodevelopment whose morphology and function evolve to meet the metabolic and waste clearance demands of the maturing brain. We integrate evidence from advanced neuroimaging, developmental neuroscience, and neurobiology studies to highlight that PVS structure and fluid dynamics may be coupled with several neurodevelopmental processes, impacted by early experiences, and mature through adolescence to facilitate healthy brain development and cognitive functioning. We advocate for longitudinal, lifespan approaches to PVS research, because understanding normative PVS development is paramount for interpreting pathological changes. This developmental reframing highlights new opportunities for early identification of at-risk individuals and preventive interventions targeting the brain's waste clearance system during sensitive developmental windows.

item.title: Enhanced Pitch Perception in Early Blind Individuals and Musicians Is due to Reduced Internal Noise.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Although it is commonly assumed that early blind individuals have enhanced pitch perception, the literature to date has been contradictory. We measured performance on two tasks known to recruit early versus late stages of auditory frequency tuning in early blind and sighted human adults of both sexes with matched years of musical training. The two groups showed equivalent performance on a tone detection in notched-noise task that assesses cochlear frequency selectivity. In contrast, early blind individuals showed enhanced performance in a pitch discrimination task thought to be mediated by cortical mechanisms. Computational modeling revealed that this enhancement was best explained by reduced internal noise rather than narrower frequency tuning, with both blindness and years of musical training predicting a reduction in internal noise. These findings identify internal noise as a key factor in experience-driven auditory plasticity as a result of both musical experience and early blindness.

item.title: Temporal Dynamics of Early Somatosensory Processing in Goal-Directed Actions.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Tactile sensitivity is temporally modulated on a moving limb. Yet the neural mechanisms underlying this modulation remain unclear. Using electroencephalography, we examined the temporal dynamics of early somatosensory processing during goal-directed reaching. Participants (self-reported gender, 22 females, 16 males) reached for their unseen left hand while a brief standard vibration of a fixed intensity was applied to the moving right index finger in different movement phases. After each reach, participants compared this standard with a second comparison vibration of varying intensity applied to the sternum and judged which vibration felt stronger. The same task was performed at rest to account for individual differences. Psychophysical results revealed an overall reduction in tactile sensitivity during reaching compared with rest, with sensitivity transiently improving around maximum speed relative to the late movement phase. Consistent with the psychophysical data, the short-latency P45 component, originating in the primary somatosensory cortex, was reduced during reaching but recovered around maximum speed. Lower P45 amplitudes were associated with lower tactile sensitivity measured behaviorally, suggesting that early somatosensory processing may contribute to the observed perceptual changes. This temporally specific modulation of tactile perception, together with corresponding changes at the early cortical stage, is consistent with the idea that the somatosensory system dynamically adapts its sensitivity to facilitate control of somatosensory-guided actions.

item.title: Opposing effects of childhood abuse and neglect on neural performance monitoring.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
The dimensional model of adversity proposes that threat (abuse) and deprivation (neglect) exert distinct effects on neurocognitive development. We tested whether these dimensions show opposing associations with neural indices of performance monitoring in a sample of 782 young adults from the CoScience EEG-Personality Project. Participants completed the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire alongside an Eriksen flanker task while electroencephalography was recorded. Performance monitoring was indexed by the error-related negativity and frontal midline theta activity. Consistent with preregistered hypotheses, abuse and neglect showed opposing associations with both neural measures. Higher abuse was associated with enhanced error-related negativity but not theta power, whereas higher neglect was associated with attenuated error-related negativity and reduced theta power. Exploratory analyses indicated that these associations were moderated by sex, with stronger effects observed in males. These findings are consistent with the distinction between threat- and deprivation-related adversity and suggest that different forms of childhood adversity may be linked to variation in neurocognitive processes underlying cognitive control. However, the cross-sectional and retrospective nature of the measures limits causal inference and may introduce reporting biases.

item.title: Temporal confounds emulate multivariate fMRI measures of perceptual learning.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Any study of learning must capture neural or behavioural changes over time. Stimuli are therefore presented more than once, before and after learning takes place-a sequence that cannot be randomised across time. This design creates vulnerability to temporal confounds that cause illusory neural effects. We investigate this issue in a classic 'one-shot' learning paradigm, in which ambiguous two-tone images become recognisable after viewing a photo cue. Across common fMRI designs, we found that spurious correlations driven by the temporal proximity of stimuli created strong artefacts in multivariate data. Among certain experimental designs, we found strong neural markers of perceptual learning depending on how stimuli were distributed across these artefacts. This paradigm-dependent effect was present not only in the primary visual cortex (V1), but also in a non-visual control region (S1), indicative of an artefactual origin rather than a genuine perceptual learning effect. We present a principled approach to correct for this temporal order confound. Once applied, the artefactual learning signature was eliminated from both V1 and S1, and while the corrected signal retained information about image identity in V1, this was absent in S1. Our work demonstrates how current multivariate neuroimaging approaches to understanding learning could be influenced by methodological artefacts that misdirect interpretations towards distributed neural processing, and offers a practical framework to distinguish true learning from measurement error.

item.title: Distinct motor preparatory signals correlate with coarse vs fine control of self-paced action timing.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Making each action at the right time is crucial for motor control. In this study, we investigated how two prominent motor preparatory processes identified in human EEG-beta-band desynchronisation and the readiness potential (RP)-might each differently relate to the time of a simple voluntary action. In our paradigm, participants learned when to act in each block of trials, based on probabilistic trial-by-trial feedback. A reward schedule reinforced a specific optimal time to act in some blocks, but allowed greater variability around the same mean action time in other blocks. We found that contralateral motor beta-band power at the beginning of each trial was higher in trials with slow actions than in those with fast actions. In contrast, contralateral beta-band power reached stereotyped low values at the time of action, regardless of waiting times. Put together, this pattern is consistent with a neural implementation of distance-to-bound for a noisy accumulation process, in which baseline motor activity starts off closer to an action-triggering bound when fast actions are required. In turn, the RP was independent of the mean waiting time before action, but its slope increased when participants developed a precise motor plan. We suggest that beta desynchronisation and the RP track distinct, complementary processes involved in the temporal control of action. While beta-power activity at trial onset is consistent with a strategic adjustment of motor preparation to match the required pace of action, the modulation of the RP by motor plan precision is consistent with a temporally structured input to a ramping preparatory process. Simulations suggest that acting at the right time may involve increasing the strength of the input to this accumulator, which can drive the decision variable to drift towards the decision bound.

item.title: Neurobehavioral correlates of changing one's mind in ADHD and OCD.
item.description:
Cerebral cortex (New York, N.Y. : 1991)
Cognitive flexibility is an executive function that allows individuals to adjust behavior in response to changing environmental demands. We assessed volitional switching under uncertainty, without rule-based learning, in the "Change Your Mind" task. Nineteen patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), 19 patients with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and matched control participants (20 per group) completed the task while undergoing a functional MRI scan. The task was a two-alternative forced choice paradigm where each stimulus was presented twice successively, with spurious feedback following the first presentation. This allowed participants the opportunity to repeat or change their response. Participants with ADHD changed their response more frequently than controls following a previously correct response, associated with reduced accuracy on the second trial. This was accompanied with smaller differences between change and repeat trials in the superior frontal gyrus, paracingulate gyrus, and frontal pole compared to controls. Participants with OCD did not differ from healthy controls in their performance but exhibited greater activity on both change and repeat trials in the pre- and postcentral gyri than controls. These results point to distinct neurobehavioral differences in patients with ADHD and OCD underlying what is often termed more broadly inflexible behavior.

item.title: Dissociating executive prefrontal substrates following capsulotomy in obsessive-compulsive disorder.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is characterized by widespread executive function impairments linked to disrupted frontostriatal circuits. Ablative therapies such as capsulotomy show promising efficacy in treatment-refractory OCD, yet their effects on executive neural substrates remain poorly understood. This study explores how OCD and capsulotomy influence executive prefrontal function. Twenty-three post-capsulotomy OCD patients, 30 OCD controls and 32 health controls (HC) were recruited in the study. Post-capsulotomy patients were recruited at least 6 months following surgery to allow for postoperative stabilization. Participants completed three executive function tasks assessing distinct cognitive domains: the Extra-Dimensional Intra-Dimensional (EDID) task testing set-shifting, the N-back task testing working memory and the Flanker task measuring conflict processing. The EDID and N-back tasks were administered during concurrent task-based functional MRI, while the Flanker task provided only behavioural measures. In the EDID task, OCD capsulotomy patients demonstrated greater post-error flexibility towards ID versus ED shifting relative to both OCD controls and HC, despite exhibiting more ED errors. OCD controls showed less shifts after errors compared with HC, which was not revealed in the capsulotomy group. OCD patients showed less neural differentiation between ED versus ID in lateral and mesial prefrontal regions relative to HC. Capsulotomy was associated with decreased pre-supplementary motor area activity to ED shifts compared with HC, indicating impairments in neural reactivity to ED shifting. No evidence supported the influence of capsulotomy in the N-back or the Flanker tasks. Specifically, both OCD groups showed impaired working memory performance at high memory load along with dysfunction in the whole frontoparietal network. In the Flanker task, impairments in dissociating congruent and incongruent conditions were found in both OCD groups but not in the HC group. These findings suggest capsulotomy specifically remediates error-monitoring and behavioural flexibility through mesial prefrontal remodelling, while leaving working memory and conflict processing deficits intact. This dissociation implies that cognitive flexibility may represent a state-dependent process amenable to intervention, whereas working memory and conflict processing impairments may reflect trait markers of OCD vulnerability. These results have clinical implications on the relative safety profile of capsulotomy and patient selection for precision neuromodulation.

item.title: Single-neuron encoding of rapidly learned visual information reshapes human perception.
item.description:
Nature neuroscience
Humans can swiftly learn to recognize visual objects after minimal exposure. Integrating new information with existing knowledge requires forming enduring neuronal representations to enable future recognition. Yet, the neuronal mechanisms in the human brain underlying such rapid perceptual changes remain unclear. Here we recorded single-neuron activity in occipital cortex (OC) and medial temporal lobe (MTL) regions as participants rapidly learned to recognize degraded images. OC and MTL neurons modulated their activity to encode newly learned visual information and reshape perception. Population decoding revealed that OC neurons required additional processing time to resolve the identity of learned images, with delayed neuronal responses in the MTL. Our findings suggest that OC supports recognition after rapid learning via extensive recurrent processing, potentially involving higher-order neocortical areas, without relying on feedback from MTL. These results provide mechanistic constraints for biologically plausible models of visual recognition and few-shot visual learning.

item.title: Physiological Representation of Social Evaluation: Modeling Human Eye Movements, Pupillary, and Neuronal Responses to Faces.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Face-based social evaluations are ubiquitous and consequential, yet it remains unclear how these evaluations are represented in spontaneous physiological responses. Across four studies (222 participants: 142 females, 57 males, 23 unreported; 503 neurons), we used a data-driven modeling framework to examine how facial appearance shapes eye movements, pupillary responses, and neuronal activity during face viewing. We asked what these responses reveal about the underlying social evaluations. Pupillary responses and hippocampal firing during saccades were driven by facial variation associated with an integrated combination of valence and power evaluations; fixation duration on the eyes and hippocampal firing during fixations were more selectively tuned to threat-related evaluations; amygdalar firing primarily tracked approachability-related valence. A prospective validation study confirmed that novel faces synthesized along these modeled directions elicited the predicted physiological responses in new participants. We also found evidence of individual differences: social anxiety selectively heightened the sensitivity of pupillary responses to face evaluations. These findings suggest that distinct physiological responses across attention, autonomic arousal, and medial temporal lobe activity reflect distinct but related facets of face-based social evaluation.Significance Statement Everyday social decisions hinge on split-second impressions of unfamiliar faces. When we see a face, we instantly judge the person's likely intention (positive ↔ negative valence) and social influence (high ↔ low power). Across four complementary studies, we show that these evaluative processes are reflected in physiological responses to faces across overt attention, autonomic arousal, and subcortical neuronal firing. Different physiological systems reflected partially distinct but related facets of social-evaluative meaning, including integrated valence-and-power, threat-related, and approachability-related evaluation.

item.title: The human hippocampus supports auditory coding and multisensory integration.
item.description:
PLoS biology
The hippocampus receives convergent input from multiple sensory systems, yet in humans it has been studied almost exclusively through vision. Here we examine how the hippocampus contributes to sensory processing beyond the visual modality and to the multisensory integration of visual information with these other modalities. Participants were exposed to multiple repetitions of short naturalistic movie clips, each presented in four formats: auditory-only, visual-only, congruent audiovisual, and incongruent audiovisual (audio and video from different movies). Using high-resolution fMRI, we measured univariate activation and multivariate representations across the longitudinal axis and subfields of the human hippocampus. Whereas univariate analyses detected only visual responses across hippocampal subregions, with no activation for auditory stimuli and no benefit of congruent stimuli, multivariate analyses revealed robust representations of both auditory and visual scenes. The posterior hippocampus showed enhanced pattern similarity for congruent stimuli relative to unisensory stimuli, especially in the left hemisphere, demonstrating multisensory facilitation. The anterior hippocampus showed crossmodal decoding between auditory and visual versions of the same clip, driven by the right hemisphere, suggesting a more abstract representation. Finally, whole-brain searchlight analyses revealed parallel effects in cortical regions known to support multisensory integration. These findings advance understanding of auditory and multisensory coding in the human hippocampus, revealing specialization and lateralization along its longitudinal axis.

item.title: Left out: The effect of handedness on fMRI activation in memory paradigms.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
About 11% of the population is left-handed, a significant minority of the potential participant pool for functional MRI (fMRI) studies. However, convention in fMRI research dictates these potential participants be excluded due to the supposition that left-handed (LH) people may have different lateralization of neural functioning than right-handed (RH) people. This difference in lateralization may cause different areas of the brain to be activated by the same task. The current study investigates the lateralization differences between LH (n = 54) and RH (n = 55) participants during encoding and recognition memory tasks for verbal and non-verbal stimuli. Additionally, we measured participants' language laterality index by administering a semantic fluency task. We found no difference between groups' behavioral memory performance for either verbal or non-verbal stimuli. Similarly, we found no group differences in fMRI activation for either verbal or non-verbal material at encoding or retrieval. When we split groups according to language lateralization, we observed more activation in right-lateralized participants for word retrieval only. To measure whether including LH in fMRI studies would dilute results, we performed Monte Carlo simulations with subsets of our data for sample sizes from n = 10 to 50 with the number of LH in each sample ranging from k = 0 to 9. Similarity metrics between activation maps for the all-RH sample and samples that include LH participants were robust, especially for large sample sizes (e.g., Dice similarity coefficients >0.9 when n = 50). Taken together, these results indicate that the inclusion of left-handed participants does not have a strong detrimental effect on memory-related fMRI activation. On this basis, we advocate for the inclusion of left-handed participants in cognitive neuroscience of memory research.

item.title: What can behavior tell us about neural dynamics?
item.description:
Trends in cognitive sciences
For decades, systems neuroscience treated behavior as an endpoint: a simplified output, such as a button press, lick, or saccade, used to isolate neural computations. Richer behavioral measurements have expanded this view by revealing neural dynamics hidden by simple outputs. Yet behavior is not a direct readout of brain activity, because similar behavioral outputs can arise from different neural mechanisms. Interpreting neural dynamics is therefore an inverse problem with no straightforward solution. Behavior can constrain this problem by exposing sensorimotor loops, narrowing plausible explanations for population activity, and formalizing neural-behavioral relationships in joint models. Together, these approaches position behavior as a principled constraint on interpreting neural dynamics and latent cognitive, affective, and computational states.

item.title: Training Interbrain Synchrony through Dyadic Neurofeedback Modulates Empathy-for-Pain.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Dyadic neurofeedback offers a socially grounded approach for modulating neural processes that unfold between interacting individuals. While recent work demonstrates that dyadic neurofeedback can enhance inter-brain synchrony during interaction, whether its effects extend beyond the trained dyad remains unclear. Here, we examined whether dyadic neurofeedback targeting inter-brain synchrony in the inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) is associated with changes in empathy-for-pain toward unfamiliar social targets. One hundred and eighty-six participants, randomly assigned to dyads, completed three neurofeedback training sessions within one week. Feedback was contingent on real-time IFG inter-brain synchrony in the neurofeedback group or on prerecorded signals in the sham-feedback control group. Empathy-for-pain was assessed before and after training. IFG inter-brain synchrony increased significantly across sessions in the neurofeedback group but not in the control group. Empathy-for-pain ratings showed different trajectories across conditions in the primary raw-data analysis, decreasing significantly in the sham-feedback group while remaining relatively stable in the neurofeedback group. A secondary analysis adjusting for a previously observed task-specific test-retest decline showed a significant increase in the neurofeedback group. Individuals with lower baseline trait empathy showed larger training-related increases in IFG inter-brain synchrony. Network analyses suggested broader changes involving IFG-IPL connectivity. Structural equation modeling further identified significant associations among training-related intra-brain synchrony, inter-brain synchrony, and empathy-for-pain change, consistent with the proposed relationship among these processes. Together, the findings indicate that dyadic neurofeedback can modulate IFG inter-brain synchrony across repeated training and may influence the trajectory of empathy-for-pain responding beyond the immediate training partner.

item.title: A Dynamic Model of Amygdala Circuits in Threat and Reward: Implications for Affective Disorders.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Animals must continuously evaluate their surroundings and select adaptive responses to survive in ever-changing environments. Central to this capacity is the assignment of importance to environmental cues, which guides motivated behavior toward rewarding opportunities and away from potential threats. Here we propose a theoretical framework, a dynamic motivational model based on threat and reward imminence, in which motivational states evolve continuously as a function of imminence rather than shifting between discrete stages. Within this framework, three interacting dimensions define the stimulus relevance of an environmental cue: salience, valence, and value. We leverage the amygdala as a substrate to illustrate the circuit mechanisms underlying importance assignment and examine how stimulus imminence drives motivational state transitions to promote adaptive behavior. Applied to affective disorders, it reframes amygdala dysfunction as projection- and circuit-specific stress adaptation rather than uniform regional hyperactivity, providing a common language for comparing major depressive disorder, anxiety disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder, and substance use disorders. By integrating animal circuit studies with human neuroimaging and clinical evidence, this framework positions amygdala-centered networks as candidate biomarkers for biologically informed subtyping and targets for personalized treatment in depression and related affective disorders.

item.title: The application of brain-computer interface on cognitive function and activities of daily living in stroke patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis
item.description:
Frontiers in neurology
来源未提供摘要。

item.title: Emotion knowledge is structured in a grid-like coordinate system in the human ventromedial prefrontal cortex.
item.description:
PLoS biology
Human emotional experiences vary widely in everyday life, yet they are systematically organized within a continuous affective space defined by valence and arousal. Although this circumplex organization has shaped decades of research, its neural implementation remains unclear. Here, we asked whether abstract emotion concepts are encoded using grid-like coordinate principles in the human brain. During fMRI, participants tracked trajectories through affective space conveyed through morphs of facial expressions and sequences of phrases. We found that ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) encoded affective space with robust hexadirectional modulation characteristic of grid-like coding. This coordinate representation generalized across stimulus modalities, indicating abstraction beyond perceptual features. The grid-like signal reflected a metric organization of emotion concepts independent of overt behavior, whereas distance-related signals in vmPFC predicted trial-by-trial affective judgements. Together, these findings suggest that emotion knowledge is structured by a grid-like coordinate system in the human brain that can support predictive inference and flexible decision-making.

item.title: Negative emotion recognition impairments despite preserved neural activity in patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI).
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Emotion recognition is an essential component of socio-emotional functioning, yet its alteration in mild cognitive impairment (MCI) remains insufficiently understood, particularly in relation to neural mechanisms. This study examined behavioral and neural responses to facial emotions in 60 adults (30 MCI, 30 healthy controls (HC)) using a validated fMRI emotion-recognition paradigm with anger, fear, sadness, happiness, and neutral expressions. Although groups did not differ in overall recognition accuracy, a multivariate analysis revealed a significant group effect driven by a selective impairment in sadness recognition in MCI. Accuracy for anger and fear showed weaker, but non-significant differences between groups, and happiness recognition was preserved. Face-processing ability, emotional interference, emotional intelligence, and domain-specific cognitive performance showed no significant associations with facial emotion recognition, indicating that the sadness-specific deficit was not attributable to perceptual, cognitive, or socio-emotional characteristics. In fMRI analyses, HCs showed widespread activation to emotional versus neutral faces across occipital, frontal, and subcortical regions, whereas patients with MCI exhibited spatially more restricted activation. However, whole-brain group comparisons revealed no significant differences in BOLD response amplitudes for overall emotion processing or any emotion-specific contrast. These findings indicate that MCI is characterized by a selective impairment in recognizing sadness, an emotion relying on subtle, low-intensity cues, while whole-brain analyses did not reveal statistically significant group differences in neural responses during emotion processing. This pattern shows that group differences in behavior did not correspond to group differences in measured neural activity.

item.title: Transcranial magnetic stimulation to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex modulates single-neuron activity in humans.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) is an established treatment for depression, yet the fundamental question of how cortical stimulation influences single neurons in deep brain circuits critical for mood regulation remains unanswered. Using a rare opportunity to record from intracranial microelectrodes while TMS was delivered in four neurosurgical patients, we evaluated the responses of 185 single neurons. Artifact cleaning enabled single-neuron spikes to be resolved as early as 8 ms after stimulation. We found that single-pulse TMS to the left dlPFC elicited time-locked firing responses in 46% of neurons (26% facilitated only, 19% suppressed only, 1% both). These responses occurred within deep bilateral cortical and subcortical structures, including the putamen and thalamus. Single-pulse TMS tended to facilitate spiking in striato-thalamic putative inhibitory neurons from ~8 ms, peaking at ~80 to 100 ms, and decaying until ~600 ms. In contrast, putative excitatory neurons and limbic areas were suppressed with a slower time course lasting to ~1,000 ms. TMS-evoked potentials recorded from intracranial depth macroelectrodes to quantify network activity revealed that the modulation of responsive neurons was positively correlated with cortico-striato-thalamic network activity and anticorrelated with limbic network activity in one participant with sufficient network and unit sampling. These results suggest that dlPFC TMS recruits a high percentage of neurons spanning cortical and subcortical brain regions bilaterally. The recruitment pattern selectively involves increasing the firing rate of inhibitory neurons in executive control networks while suppressing limbic excitatory drive, providing a candidate cellular mechanism for how cortical stimulation modulates distributed brain networks.

item.title: A causal account of the neural origins of mental fatigue.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Successful goal-directed behavior often requires the exertion of effortful cognitive control processes, but it remains unclear why engaging in cognitive control is experienced as effortful and induces fatigue. Here, we tested the hypothesis that sustained activation in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC)-a neural substrate of cognitive control-causally induces motivational fatigue via the accumulation of prefrontal glutamate metabolites. For this purpose, we combined brain stimulation with spectroscopy imaging to assess how increasing DLPFC excitability during an effortful mental task changes the motivation for mental effort and glutamate concentrations. We found that stimulating the DLPFC during mental effort exertion improved mental performance at the cost of increased posteffort motivational fatigue, suggesting a causal role of DLPFC activation for inducing fatigue. On the neural level, DLPFC activation during effortful cognition also increased prefrontal concentrations of glutamate, which statistically explained the fatigue-induced lower motivation for mental effort. A corresponding analysis of combined glutamate-glutamine (Glx) concentrations revealed converging effects. Together, these findings provide causal evidence that enhanced DLPFC activation contributes to fatigue via neurochemical changes, supporting neuro-metabolic accounts of fatigue and offering new insights into why demanding cognitive tasks are perceived as effortful.

item.title: State-Dependent EEG Markers of Excitation/Inhibition and Hemodynamic State Are Associated with Random Noise Stimulation Effects.
item.description:
NeuroImage
